title: Agent City — The Web Built for Humans and Agents
pitch: A miniature internet built from the ground up for humans and AI agents to navigate, collaborate, and act together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A miniature internet built from the ground up for humans and AI agents to navigate, collaborate, and act together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Agent City: An Agent-Native Web Experiment The web was made for people. Every button, form, and checkout flow assumes a human is staring at the screen and deciding what to click. AI agents are changing that, but most current browser agents just mimic humans. They inspect a page, find an element, click it, and wait for the result. It is a slow, repetitive loop. We wanted to see what happens when agents are treated as first-class users. So we built Agent City , a small, simulated internet where humans and AI agents work together. The event planning scenario is just an easy way to show the concept, but the real experiment is about what an “agent-native” web actually looks like. The Four Districts Agent City has four districts: Venue District: Searches for and reserves spaces. Catering District: Finds food based on headcounts and budgets. Calendar District: Manages scheduling. Budget District: Tracks spending. Humans use a standard visual UI. Agents use WebMCP tools such as search_venues() and schedule_event() . Both interfaces interact with the same underlying state. How It Works If a user asks for a vegetarian meetup for 12 people tomorrow after 2 PM under ₹10,000, the agent finds the venue and food, checks the budget, and builds the plan. Things get interesting when requirements change. If the guest list jumps to 20 and the venue only holds 15, the system flags the conflict. The agent then has to find a bigger venue and redo the catering and budget. It is not just browser automation; it is collaboration over shared data. To make this visible, we added: An Agent Activity Graph A WebMCP Inspector These tools allow humans to see the agent’s work in real time. Technology We built the city using: React TypeScript Vite Cloudflare Workers D1 The architecture is straightforward: $$ \text{Human} \rightarrow \text{Visual Interface} \rightarrow \text{Shared State} \rightarrow \text{WebMCP Layer} \rightarrow \text{AI Agent} $$ Designing the Tools Instead of one giant “do everything” tool, we gave agents small, composable capabilities. We also made these tools context-aware. An agent sees reserve_venue() before a booking exists, but sees modify_reservation() once the booking is made. The hardest part was the tool design. A tool needs: A clear name A predictable result A well-defined purpose If tools overlap, the agent gets confused. If they are too broad, the agent stops reasoning. If they are too small, the task takes too many calls. Keeping Humans and Agents in Sync We also had to keep the human and agent views in sync. When an agent books a venue, the UI has to show it immediately. When a human changes the attendee count, the agent has to react to that new state. We found that building for agents does not mean killing the UI. Humans and agents just need different views of the same world: Humans want visual exploration and direct control. Agents want typed inputs and predictable results. What Comes Next Agent City is currently focused on event planning, but the idea could work for anything from finance to infrastructure. Next, we want to explore: Better permission systems Human approval flows More complex agent collaboration Safer handling of high-impact actions The core question is simple. If agents are now normal participants on the web, why force them to use interfaces made only for humans? Built With chatgpt cloudflare css html javascript react typescript vite webmcp Try it out github.com agent-city.imyash-chaudhary2.workers.dev Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I built the entire project solo — frontend, backend, and agent layer. I designed and built Agent City as a WebMCP-native app: a React + TypeScript frontend where every capability is exposed as a typed tool through document.modelContext, backed by a Cloudflare Worker API. The hardest part was the tool surface design — getting the read/write annotations, dynamic registration (tools appear only when state unlocks them), and the human-in-the-loop approval gate to all stay consistent. I learned that designing for agents is a different discipline from designing UIs: the schema is the interface, and the approval flow is a UX problem, not just a security check.
